name: Raw carrot salad (Ray Peat)

image.caption: Raw Carrot Salad, Grilled Vermont Cheddar, Carrot Ginger Soup

lead: The raw carrot salad is a shredded carrot with oil, vinegar and salt, eaten daily by followers of Ray Peat's bioenergetic diet.
People use it hoping for clearer skin, less bloating and a leaner look, and many simply enjoy it as an inexpensive side dish.

paras: Followers say carrot fibre helps carry endotoxin and excess estrogen out of the gut, which they link to better skin and body composition. Carrots also supply fibre and carotenoids that can warm skin tone.
Generally a low-risk food. Large amounts of carotenoids may tint the skin orange, and raw fibre can cause gas in some people. No clinical trial has tested the protocol.

web.title: Ray Peat, PhD on the Benefits of the Raw Carrot
The Viral Carrot Salad: On Ray Peat and the Science

chain: Fibre and carotenoids reach the gut and skin
Clearer, warmer-looking complexion as described by followers
angle.text: Followers eat a shredded raw carrot with oil and vinegar each day, reasoning that it supports gut and hormone balance and in turn skin clarity and a leaner look. Carotenoid-rich foods are also discussed for a warmer skin tone.

lead: The raw carrot salad is a daily food habit associated with the bioenergetic diet popularised by the American biologist Ray Peat. It is a grated or shredded raw carrot dressed with a little oil, vinegar and salt, eaten as a side dish between meals or with one. Followers describe it as a gut-and-hormone routine that they connect to clearer skin, less bloating and a leaner, less puffy look [1][2].

In Peat's account as relayed by his followers, raw carrot fibre stimulates the intestine and keeps estrogen that the liver sends into bile from being reabsorbed, while the vinegar and oil dressing is said to suppress bacterial growth and lower endotoxin absorption. One widely shared line has Peat describing his basic approach as lowering estrogen and stress hormones by diet, including a daily carrot salad [1]. Followers link lower gut endotoxin and estrogen to better skin, hair and body composition, and carrots also supply beta-carotene, which can warm skin tone when carotenoid intake is high.

Research on dietary fibre and estrogen excretion exists, and some small studies are described in a recent review of the salad; no published human trial has tested the carrot salad itself [2]. It spread from Peat-diet circles into wellness blogs and social media recipes, usually under the label of hormone balance [2].
infobox: Grated raw carrot, oil, vinegar, salt [1]
Grated carrots, vinegar, coconut oil and salt [1]
Between meals, usually in the afternoon [1]

paras: The salad is a small portion of raw carrot, grated or cut into thin strips, dressed with a modest amount of oil, a splash of vinegar and some salt. Peat's recipe essentials, as quoted by a supplement-industry blog, are grated carrots, vinegar, coconut oil and salt [1]. Peat-diet communities treat it as a staple alongside foods such as orange juice, milk and cooked mushrooms.

The Frondescent article describes the basic version as one shredded carrot with oil, vinegar and salt, and shows its author's variant that adds shredded radish, crushed garlic and extra-virgin olive oil. The author explains that olive oil stays fluid when the salad cools, whereas coconut oil turns waxy, that fat aids carotene absorption, and that crushing garlic and letting it rest produces allicin before the vinegar is added [2].
Peat is quoted as saying the carrots must be raw for the intended effect, that it takes a few days for the intestine to adjust to raw carrot, and that the salad is best eaten between meals [1].

The salad is attributed to Raymond Peat, an American biologist with a 1972 PhD from the University of Oregon whose dissertation concerned age-related oxidative changes in the hamster uterus; he was not a physician and did not run clinical trials, and spent much of his later career writing independently [2]. His writing on hormones, metabolism and ageing circulated for decades outside mainstream medicine.

A September 2012 post on the Functional Performance Systems blog collected his comments on the raw carrot. Its commenters were told that one quote came from Peat's book Nutrition for Women, written in the 1970s, and that his views have evolved since; the blog said its own experience supported the carrot theory [1]. In the 2020s the salad was widely reposted on social media with claims about clearing excess estrogen, easing constipation and balancing hormones [2].

On looksmax.org, Peat's diet is discussed in resource lists, threads on his view of sodium and water retention, members' notes on the diet, and threads pairing it with other food-philosophy figures [3][4][5][6][7][8]. A 2023-era WTOP explainer, 'Ray Peat Diet: What Is It, and Does It Work?', was shared on Hacker News in March 2024.

According to the 2012 post quoting Peat, the claim has several parts. Fibre is said to reduce absorption of bacterial toxins (endotoxin) from the intestine, and a grated carrot with salt and vinegar is credited with reducing endotoxin absorption. Fibre is said to prevent the reabsorption of estrogen secreted in bile, shifting balance toward progesterone and thyroid function within days. Peat is quoted as saying the salad improves the ratio of progesterone to estrogen and cortisol [1].

He also said a daily carrot salad can stimulate and disinfect the small intestine enough to prevent fermentation, that carrot fibre binds fat and carries it out, and that the sugar in carrots is released slowly [1]. The post says Peat noted that carrots' natural antibacterial action might call for occasional vitamin K from liver or broccoli, that excess carotene may inhibit progesterone synthesis, and that bamboo shoots and carrots are, in his view, a safe way to keep endotoxin and estrogen under control [1].

Peat is further quoted as saying a daily raw carrot prevented his own migraines, and as proposing the salad for PMS and gout [1]. These are Peat's statements as relayed by the blog, and the post notes that some draw on older writings [1].

sections.h: Related research on fibre and estrogen
paras: The underlying biology that the liver tags estrogen for removal and gut bacteria can strip the tag so it is reabsorbed is established. The Frondescent review cites a 1982 observational study of 10 vegetarian and 10 omnivorous premenopausal women in which vegetarians ate more fibre, produced more stool and excreted more estrogen in faeces; a study of 62 premenopausal women in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition in which serum estrone and estradiol fell only in the wheat-bran group, not with oat or corn bran; and a British Journal of Cancer study in which faster transit with wheat bran, senna or loperamide was associated with lower estrogen measures while faecal beta-glucuronidase did not change significantly [2].

It adds an in-vitro digestion study in which olive oil increased carotenoid bioaccessibility from carrots, a crossover feeding trial of 70 people in Cancer Prevention Research in which cruciferous and apiaceous vegetable diets affected bilirubin, an indirect marker of the estrogen-conjugating enzyme UGT1A1, with results varying by genotype, and an analysis of GLP-1 medication users in which delayed gastric emptying was more common than delayed whole-gut transit [2]. None of these tested the salad or measured estrogen after eating it [2].

The article concludes that the salad is not a proven treatment for estrogen excess, acne, PMS, constipation or any hormonal condition, that Peat's idea 'remains a hypothesis', and that its author still values it as a way to eat raw vegetables with fat. The author advises people with bloating or fullness on GLP-1 medications to start with small portions [2].

Proponents say the fibre in raw carrot binds or speeds clearance of estrogen and gut endotoxin, reducing what they regard as a drag on thyroid function and skin quality [1]. Users report smoother skin, less bloating and a sharper facial outline.

On looksmax.org, Ray Peat's diet is discussed in threads including a resource list on metabolic rate and hormones, one on his view of sodium and water retention, one titled 'ray peat seems legit so far', and members' notes on the diet [3][4][5][6]. Other threads dispute him, such as one calling his popularity a 'psyop' [9], and members have posted thyroid test results seeking advice [10]. Another thread pairs Peat with the primal-diet author Aajonus Vonderplanitz as a combined 'stack' [8].

No studies found on the carrot salad as Peat's followers describe it. General research on dietary fibre and estrogen excretion exists, and the studies described above were of broader categories; the Frondescent article states that no published human trial shows the salad lowers estrogen or removes endotoxin [2].

Very high carotenoid intake can give the skin a yellow-orange tint (carotenemia), which is harmless and fades when intake falls. Raw fibre can cause gas or loose stools in people unaccustomed to it, and Peat is quoted as saying the intestine needs a few days to adjust [1]. The Frondescent author suggests people with fullness on GLP-1 drugs start small, omit garlic if it causes bloating and not use more fibre to counter severe symptoms [2].

Peat's diet, as summarised in a looksmax.org post quoting a dietitian, emphasises dairy, fruit and juice, root vegetables, collagen and eggs, and avoids polyunsaturated fats; the carrot salad is one of its signature items [11]. Forum members also circulate claims about Peat's own health and body, including a thread asserting he gained height with DHEA in his 40s, which a reply doubted given his other bold claims [12]. These are community discussions rather than research findings.

lore.intro: The carrot salad is mentioned in Peat-influenced communities as a daily staple, and looksmax.org members discuss Peat's diet for hormones and water retention.[3][4]

timeline.event: Peat's book Nutrition for Women, from which one widely quoted carrot passage is said to derive, is written. [1]
Ray Peat earns a biology PhD at the University of Oregon. [2]
An observational study of vegetarian and omnivorous women finds higher faecal estrogen with higher fibre intake, later cited in discussions of the salad. [2]
Functional Performance Systems publishes a collection of Peat's quotes on the benefits of raw carrot (28 September). [1]
The carrot salad is reposted widely on social media as a hormone-balance recipe. [2]
A WTOP explainer on the Ray Peat diet is shared on Hacker News (March).
